lede: Tilt a floor far enough and a box that was sitting still starts to slide. Nothing new pushes it: the weight is the same as before, but part of it now points along the surface. Splitting the weight into those two parts is the whole of this topic.
can: Resolve a weight into its components along and perpendicular to a slope
Decide which component takes the sine, from the shape of the problem rather than a mnemonic
Write the equation of motion for a body going up a slope and for the same body coming down

text: Why a slope is harder than a floor

md: On level ground the weight points straight down and the surface pushes straight up, so they simply cancel. Tilt the surface and the weight no longer lines up with anything, and part of it starts pulling the body along the slope.

text: 1. Turn the axes onto the slope

alt: A block on a slope at angle alpha. Friction F acts up the slope, along the plane; the normal reaction R acts at right angles to the plane; the weight mg acts straight down, along neither.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='300'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M26 270L366 73.7L366 270Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.07' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M72 270A46 46 0 0 0 65.8 247' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='80' y='262' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>α</text><path d='M164.8 189.9L227.2 153.9L202.2 110.5L139.8 146.5Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M214.7 132.2L264.9 103.2' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M264.9 103.2L258.3 111.8L254.1 104.6Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='257.4' y='89.1' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>F</text><path d='M171 128.5L142 78.3' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M142 78.3L150.6 84.9L143.4 89.1Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='134' y='80.3' text-anchor='end' font-size='15'>R</text><path d='M183.5 150.2L183.5 228.2' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M183.5 228.2L179.3 218.2L187.7 218.2Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='191.5' y='226.2' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>mg</text></g></svg>
caption: The friction and the reaction already lie along the two new axes; only the weight does not.

md: Instead of horizontal and vertical, use **along the plane** and **perpendicular to it**. The motion, the friction and any applied force already lie along the plane, and the normal reaction already lies perpendicular to it. That leaves the weight as the single force that has to be broken up.

prompt: On an inclined plane, which force is the one that has to be resolved into components?
explain: With the axes turned onto the slope, the friction lies along one axis and the normal reaction along the other, as the picture shows. The weight points straight down, along neither, so the weight is the one to resolve.

text: 2. Where the sine and cosine come from

alt: The weight mg drawn straight down from a point on a slope at angle alpha, with its two components dashed: mg sin alpha down the slope and mg cos alpha into it, completing a rectangle. The angle alpha is marked at the foot of the slope and again between the weight and the component into the slope.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='300'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M24 274L376 70.8L376 274Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.06' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M68 274A44 44 0 0 0 62.1 252' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='76' y='266' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>α</text><path d='M141 139.5L192.1 228L243.2 198.5' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='3 3' stroke-opacity='0.6'/><circle cx='192.1' cy='110' r='3.5' fill='currentColor'/><path d='M192.1 110L192.1 228' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2.2'/><path d='M192.1 228L187.9 218L196.3 218Z' fill='currentColor'/><path d='M192.1 110L141 139.5' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><path d='M141 139.5L147.6 130.8L151.8 138.1Z' fill='currentColor'/><path d='M192.1 110L243.2 198.5' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><path d='M243.2 198.5L234.6 191.9L241.9 187.7Z' fill='currentColor'/><path d='M192.1 140A30 30 0 0 0 207.1 135.9' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='205.5' y='158.5' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>α</text><text x='184.1' y='232' text-anchor='end' font-size='15'>mg</text><text x='133' y='137.5' text-anchor='end' font-size='15'>mg sin α</text><text x='251.2' y='202.5' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>mg cos α</text></g></svg>
caption: The weight and its two parts: the angle α appears again between the weight and the part into the slope.

md: The plane is at $\alpha$ to the horizontal, so the line perpendicular to it is at $\alpha$ to the vertical: turning both lines through $90°$ keeps the angle between them. The weight is vertical, so it makes the angle $\alpha$ with the perpendicular. In the right-angled triangle it builds, the side next to $\alpha$ is $mg\cos\alpha$, into the slope, and the side opposite is $mg\sin\alpha$, along it.

**Shown:** a 9 kg box on a 25° slope, weight $90$ N.
**Along the slope:** $90\sin 25° = 38.04$ N, the side opposite $\alpha$.
**Into the slope:** $90\cos 25° = 81.57$ N, the side next to it.

prompt: A body of weight 80 N rests on a slope at 30°. What is the component of its weight along the slope, in newtons?
explain: Along the slope is the side opposite $\alpha$ in the weight's triangle, so it takes the sine, as the 9 kg box above did: $80\sin 30° = 80 \times 0.5 = 40$ N. The cosine gives 69.28 N, the part pressing into the slope.

text: 3. Why the flat-slope check never fails

md: Rebuild the rule rather than memorise it. Imagine the slope almost flat. The body would barely slide, so the part along the slope is nearly zero, and $\sin 0° = 0$. The ground would take nearly the whole weight, so the part into the slope is nearly $mg$, and $\cos 0° = 1$.

title: Why the check is worth more than the rule
md: A remembered rule is the first thing to go under pressure, and this is the most repeated slip on the topic. The flat-slope test rebuilds both components from something you cannot forget: a flat floor holds a body up and lets it slide nowhere.

prompt: A slope is made steeper and steeper, until it is almost vertical. Which part of the weight becomes nearly the whole weight?
explain: Run the flat-slope check the other way: as the slope steepens towards $90°$, $\sin\alpha$ grows towards 1 and $\cos\alpha$ shrinks towards 0. So the part along the slope becomes nearly the whole weight: the body is nearly falling freely, and the surface barely touches it.

md: A body accelerating on a slope is not in equilibrium, but it is not far off. Perpendicular to the plane the forces always balance, because nothing sinks into the surface or lifts off it, so $R = mg\cos\alpha$. Along the plane there is a resultant, and that is where the acceleration comes from.

prompt: A body is accelerating down a rough slope. Which statement is true?
options: The perpendicular forces balance but the along-slope forces do not
The along-slope forces balance but the perpendicular ones do not
answer: The perpendicular forces balance but the along-slope forces do not
explain: The body does not sink into the slope or lift off it, so across the slope the forces balance and $R = mg\cos\alpha$. Along the slope it is speeding up, so there is a resultant there; if everything balanced there would be no acceleration.

text: 4. The two things CCEA fixes for you

caption: The pull P is parallel to the plane, and the friction F is a number you are given.

md: Two restrictions make this topic smaller than it looks on other boards. An applied force **always acts parallel to the plane**, so it never needs resolving, and friction is always **given as a value**: $F = \mu R$ is not on this specification. The normal reaction still belongs on every diagram.

prompt: On a CCEA inclined-plane question, in which direction does an externally applied force act?
options: At whatever angle the question chooses
explain: The Teacher Guidance restricts it in terms: any push or pull on a CCEA slope acts parallel to the plane, as P does in the picture. That is why the weight is the only force you ever resolve here.

alt: A box of mass 12 kilograms on a slope at 25 degrees to the horizontal. Friction of 20 newtons acts up the slope, the normal reaction R acts out of the slope, the weight of 120 newtons acts straight down, and a dashed arrow shows the acceleration down the slope.

caption: Weight 120 N, friction 20 N, and the box on its way down.

md:
**A 12 kg box sliding down a 25° slope against 20 N of friction.**
**Perpendicular:** $R = 120\cos 25°$, so $R = 108.76$ N.
**Along, down positive:** $120\sin 25° = 50.71$ N pulls it down; friction opposes with 20 N.
**So:** $50.71 - 20 = 12a$, giving $a = 2.56$ m/s².

prompt: A 7 kg crate slides down a 30° slope against 14 N of friction. What is its acceleration, in m/s²? Take $g = 10$ m/s².
explain: Sliding down, the weight's part along the slope drives and friction opposes, as for the 12 kg box above. Here $70\sin 30° = 35$ N, so $35 - 14 = 7a$ and $a = 3$ m/s².

alt: A block of mass 8 kilograms pushed up a slope at 25 degrees by a force of 70 newtons parallel to the plane, with friction of 12 newtons down the slope, the normal reaction out of the slope, the weight of 80 newtons straight down, and a dashed arrow showing the acceleration up the slope.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='300'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M26 270L366 111.5L366 270Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.07' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M72 270A46 46 0 0 0 67.7 250.6' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='80' y='262' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>25°</text><path d='M163.4 205.9L228.6 175.5L207.5 130.2L142.2 160.6Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='185.4' y='163.1' text-anchor='middle' font-size='14' font-weight='600'>8 kg</text><path d='M218.1 152.9L270.6 128.3' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M270.6 128.3L263.3 136.4L259.8 128.8Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='265' y='113.4' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>70 N</text><path d='M152.8 183.3L100.2 207.8' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M100.2 207.8L107.5 199.8L111.1 207.4Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='87.3' y='192.9' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>12 N</text><path d='M174.9 145.4L150.4 92.8' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M150.4 92.8L158.4 100.1L150.8 103.7Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='142.4' y='94.8' text-anchor='end' font-size='15'>R</text><path d='M185.4 168.1L185.4 246.1' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M185.4 246.1L181.2 236.1L189.6 236.1Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='193.4' y='244.1' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>80 N</text><path d='M201.6 98.7L237.9 81.8' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><path d='M237.9 81.8l-6.7 9.2M237.9 81.8l-11.4 -0.8' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4'/><text x='213' y='79.8' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>a</text></g></svg>
caption: A 70 N push up the slope, with the weight's part and 12 N of friction against it.

md: The push is parallel to the plane, so only the weight needs resolving. The block moves up, so friction and the weight's part along the slope both act down it, against the push.

prompt: A 4 kg block is pulled up a slope at 20° to the horizontal by a 40 N force parallel to the plane, against 6 N of friction. What is its acceleration, in m/s², to 2 decimal places? Take $g = 10$ m/s².
explain: Going up, the weight's part and the friction both act against the pull, as for the block above. Only the weight is resolved: it is $4 \times 10 = 40$ N, and its part down the slope is $40\sin 20° = 13.68$ N. So $40 - 13.68 - 6 = 4a$ and $a = 5.08$ m/s².

alt: The same block on the same slope twice. On the left it slides down, with a dashed arrow showing the motion down the slope and friction F pointing up it. On the right it moves up, and friction F points down the slope.

caption: Change the direction of travel and exactly one arrow moves: the friction.

md: Friction opposes the motion, so it points up the slope when the body slides down and down the slope when the body moves up. Nothing else on the diagram changes. That is why a body always slows harder going up than it speeds up coming down: going up, the weight's part and friction add.

prompt: The same block on the same rough slope is released to slide down, and then projected up. Which is larger in size?
explain: Look at the two pictures: only friction turns round. Going up, the weight's part and friction both point down the slope and add; coming down, friction works against the weight's part. So the deceleration going up is the larger.

md:
**A 6 kg block on a 35° slope, with 10 N of friction either way.** Its weight's part along the slope is $60\sin 35° = 34.41$ N.
**Down the slope:** $34.41 - 10 = 6a$, so $a = 4.07$ m/s².
**Up the slope:** $34.41 + 10 = 6a$, so the deceleration is $7.40$ m/s².
Take the resultant in the direction of travel each time, and both come out as positive sizes.

title: FM Mechanics Incline Plane
why: Taught against this specification by name, so its restrictions are built in. Watch the axes go onto the slope before any force is resolved.

prompt: A 5 kg body is projected up a 30° slope against 10 N of friction. What is its deceleration, in m/s²? Take $g = 10$ m/s².
explain: Going up, the friction adds to the weight's part, as in the "up the slope" line above: $50\sin 30° = 25$ N, so $25 + 10 = 5a$ and the deceleration is 7 m/s².

alt: A block of mass 6 kilograms moving up a slope at 22 degrees with no push. Friction of 15 newtons acts down the slope, the normal reaction R out of the slope and the weight of 60 newtons straight down; a dashed arrow shows the acceleration pointing down the slope, against the motion.

caption: Moving up with no push: the weight's part and friction both slow it.

md: A block sent up a slope has no push. The weight's part along the slope and the friction both act down it, so the block decelerates, and a constant-acceleration formula then says how far it goes before it stops.

**Against the motion:** $60\sin 22° + 15$, which is 37.48 N.
**Deceleration:** $37.48 = 6a$, so $a = 6.25$ m/s².
**Distance to stop from 9 m/s:** $0 = 9^2 - 2 \times 6.25 \times s$, so $s = 6.48$ m.

prompt: A block moving up a slope at 6 m/s decelerates at 4 m/s². How far up the slope does it travel before it stops, in metres?
explain: It stops, so $v = 0$, and a deceleration of 4 means $a = -4$, as in the stopping line above: $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ gives $0 = 6^2 - 2 \times 4 \times s$, so $8s = 36$ and $s = 4.5$ m.

alt: A box sliding down a rough slope at angle alpha with exactly three forces: the weight mg straight down, the normal reaction R at right angles to the slope, and friction F up the slope. A dashed open arrow down the slope shows the acceleration, which is not a force.

caption: A box sliding down a rough slope carries three forces, and none of them is drawn along the slope downwards.

md: **Mark the forces** (2021, 2024, 2025). Three arrows: the weight straight down, the reaction at right angles to the slope, and friction against the motion. $mg\sin\alpha$ is part of the weight, not a fourth force.

prompt: A box slides down a rough slope. A student marks four forces on it: the weight straight down, the normal reaction, friction up the slope, and a force pulling it down the slope. Which arrow should not be there?
explain: The picture above has three forces and no more. The pull down the slope is the weight's own component, and the weight is already drawn, so drawing it again counts it twice. The 2024 report saw that extra arrow often, and an extra force costs the diagram mark.

md: **Kinematics at either end** (2021, 2024, 2025). A stopping distance may come first, giving the deceleration before any force (2021), or a speed or distance may come last, from your acceleration. First line: decide which way round.
**A value to show** (2021, 2024). A deceleration or a friction force is printed for you to show. The equation goes in with the letter in it; the value must come out, not go in.

**Shown:** a 6 kg box moving up a 20° slope against 9 N; show the deceleration is 5 to the nearest whole number.
**Up positive:** $-60\sin 20° - 9 = 6a$
**So:** $-29.52 = 6a$, $a = -4.92$: a deceleration of 5, the printed value last.

prompt: A part says: show that the deceleration of the box up the slope is 4 m/s², to the nearest whole number. What should your working do?
options: Form the equation of motion and solve it for a
Put a = 4 into the equation and check that it balances
Quote v = u + at with a = 4
answer: Form the equation of motion and solve it for a
explain: A show-that is marked on the method: the equation formed with $a$ still in it, then solved, so the printed value comes out last, as the 6 kg box above reached 5. The 2024 report saw many put the given value into an equation instead; only the full method earned full marks.

md: **The return journey** (2021, 2024). After stopping, the block slides back down and friction turns round. First line: a new equation, down the slope positive.
**Friction per kilogram** (2025). The friction is given in newtons per kilogram of mass. First line: multiply by the body's own mass before it goes into the equation.

**Shown:** 2 N per kg on a 9 kg box sliding down a 30° slope.
**Friction:** $2 \times 9 = 18$ N
**Equation:** $45 - 18 = 9a$, so $a = 3$ m/s².
**Which option wins** (2019). Two ways to move one block are compared, say sliding down or pulled up. First line: each acceleration in its own direction of travel; then compare sizes.

prompt: A 7 kg box slides down a rough slope, and the friction is given as 3 N per kg of mass. What goes into the equation of motion for the friction?
explain: Per kilogram means every kilogram of the box is resisted by 3 N, so multiply by its own mass, as the 9 kg box above did: $3 \times 7 = 21$ N.

text: 11. Going further: up, stop and back

alt: A block of mass 5 kilograms sliding back down a slope at 20 degrees, between the point B near the top where it stopped and the point A near the foot where it started. Friction F now acts up the slope, the normal reaction R out of the slope, the weight of 50 newtons straight down, and a dashed arrow shows the acceleration down the slope.

caption: On the way back down, friction has turned round to act up the slope.

md: The hardest shape so far (2021) runs the whole trip: up, stop, and back to the start. Here a 5 kg block leaves $A$ at 6 m/s up a 20° slope and stops at $B$, 3.6 m further up.

**Deceleration from the trip up:** $0 = 6^2 - 2a \times 3.6$, so $a = 5$ m/s².
**Friction:** $50\sin 20° + F = 5 \times 5$, so $F = 7.90$ N.
**Back down, friction up:** $17.10 - 7.90 = 5a$, so $a = 1.84$ m/s².
**Speed back at A:** $v^2 = 2 \times 1.84 \times 3.6$, so $v = 3.64$ m/s.

prompt: After stopping, a 4 kg block slides back down a 30° slope against 6 N of friction. What is its acceleration, in m/s²? Take $g = 10$ m/s².
explain: On the way back down, friction turns round to act up the slope, as in the picture above, while the weight's part still acts down it: $40\sin 30° = 20$ N, so $20 - 6 = 4a$ and $a = 3.5$ m/s².

title: Where the specification stops
md: Friction as $F = \mu R$, a force at an angle to the plane, and two connected bodies on a slope are A-level mechanics. CCEA's slopes carry one body, with any push parallel to the plane and the friction given.

Rotate the axes onto the slope and resolve the weight: $mg\sin\alpha$ along, $mg\cos\alpha$ across.
Rebuild which part takes the sine from the flat-slope test.
Find $R$ from perpendicular balance, and the acceleration along the plane.
Write the equation for each direction of travel, with friction turned round.
Spot the twists: the diagram, kinematics at either end, a value to show, the return trip, friction per kilogram.

Most years this is a whole question: mark the forces, find the normal reaction or show a value, write the equation of motion, then the return trip or a speed or a distance. The equation earns one mark for the resultant along the slope, resolved with the sine, and one for $= ma$; the last is the value, positive in the direction of travel. Stuck? Axes on the slope first, then the direction of motion.
